title: Role of dissipation dilution in achieving high mechanical quality factors in van der Waals resonators
authors: Lukas Schleicher, Leonard Geilen, Alexander Musta, Niklas Walter, Anne Rodriguez, Philipp Bredol, Alexander W. Holleitner, Eva M. Weig
abstract: Dissipation dilution has driven a revolution in the quality factors ($Q$) of top-down nanomechanical resonators. Yet it has not been leveraged for van der Waals (vdW) materials. Here we report quality factors up to $372{,}000\pm37{,}000$ in monolayer MoS$_2$ drums at 4 K, nearly an order of magnitude beyond the previous best for any vdW material at this temperature, enabled by a clean, polymer-free exfoliation technique. We develop a dissipation-dilution model for circular drums and analyze the contributing intrinsic and extrinsic dissipation mechanisms. The MoS$_2$ monolayer exhibits a dilution factor of order $1,000$, establishing sub-nanometer-thin resonators as ultimate dilution materials. The intrinsic quality factor, however, is limited by surface losses at atomic thickness. Conversely, multilayer drums show a lower dilution factor but a high intrinsic quality factor, on par with established top-down materials of similar dimensions, both resulting from the increased thickness. A two-level-system analysis of the temperature-dependent damping confirms this bulk-versus-surface picture and provides first insight into its microscopic origin. Our results identify dissipation dilution as the governing mechanism for high-$Q$ mechanical vdW resonators. Combined with strategies such as soft clamping or stress engineering, they establish atomically thin resonators as a platform for ultrahigh-$Q$ quantum transduction and sensing.
summary: This paper investigates how mechanical quality factors in van der Waals resonators are enhanced by a mechanism called dissipation dilution. Using MoS2 drums, the authors report record-high Q factors by modeling the energy dissipation in circular membranes. The findings establish that dissipation dilution is the key factor enabling ultra-high-Q resonators, paving the way for quantum transduction applications.
main_problem: To establish and quantify the role of "dissipation dilution" in achieving record-high mechanical quality factors (Q) in atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) resonators.
main_result: The study reports record Q factors up to 372,000 in monolayer MoS2 drums, demonstrating that dissipation dilution is the governing mechanism for high-Q mechanical response in these ultra-thin materials.
method: The authors combine rigorous theoretical modeling of energy dissipation in circular drums with experimental measurements using optical interferometry in a cryostat.
model_or_system: The system is a suspended circular drum made of vdW materials like MoS2, analyzed using an elastic energy balance model that decomposes Q into intrinsic and dilution components. The model is adapted for the axisymmetric mode shapes of the drum geometry.
key_observables: Quality factor (Q), Dilution Factor (D), Intrinsic Quality Factor (Q_int), and fundamental eigenfrequency (f_0).
important_parameters: Temperature (4 K), material thickness (monolayer vs. multilayer), and the ratio of stored elastic energy contributions.
main_assumptions: The intrinsic quality factor of monolayers is limited by surface losses at atomic thickness, and the model assumes the applicability of the energy balance approach for the circular geometry.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows the experimental setup and a measurement yielding Q ~ 229,000 for a monolayer drum. Figure 3 compares Q vs. radius for monolayer and multilayer drums, illustrating the interplay between D and Q_int.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical model for dissipation dilution in circular drums, presents experimental measurements on MoS2 drums at cryogenic temperatures, and analyzes the trade-off between high dilution factors (monolayer) and high intrinsic quality factors (multilayer).
why_interesting: The work connects macroscopic mechanical properties (high Q) to fundamental material physics (vdW bonding, surface losses) and provides a quantitative framework (dissipation dilution) applicable to nanoscale quantum devices.
